question: Within the same island, are colony pairs that are more often counted on the exact same dates more synchronous, as expected under a simple shared census-batch error explanation?

data.pair_inclusion: same-island colony-code pairs with at least 4 shared observed adjacent-year growth intervals and non-zero growth variance
data.missingness: no missing-as-zero and no colony-code merging

primary_predictor.name: same_both_endpoint_fraction
primary_predictor.definition: among shared growth intervals for a colony pair, fraction where the two colonies have the same census date at both t-1 and t
primary_predictor.expected_under_simple_batch_error: positive association with Fisher-z transformed pairwise growth correlation

null.construction: within every island-year, independently permute observed census dates among colony codes while leaving counts, missingness and annual growth attached to the original codes
null.purpose: preserve island-year timing distributions and all demographic trajectories while breaking code-specific same-date pairing

decision_rule.support_simple_same_day_batch_pattern: focal coefficient > 0 and empirical upper-tail permutation p <= 0.05
decision_rule.otherwise: report no evidence that exact same-day co-counting explains stronger within-island synchrony; do not claim all observation error is ruled out

boundaries: A positive timing slope would be compatible with batch error but could also reflect spatially clustered census routes or biological proximity.
A null/negative slope addresses exact same-day timing only; observer identity, protocol-wide error and island-wide environmental shocks remain possible.
Do not tune date similarity definitions, pair overlap thresholds, model covariates or permutation scheme after opening the result.
